title: Service Reliability Governance and SLO Runbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document defines the governance model, measurable SLOs and error-budget policy, capacity planning practices, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and a set of primary runbooks used by the eng-sre team. It is intended for SREs, service owners, and platform engineers responsible for reliability across Redwood Inference services.

Scope
- Public-facing and internal production services (API gateway, inference-serving, routing service, billing/usage pipelines).
- Applies to Redwood hosted and Dedicated deployments; customers running Private deployments should follow this governance template and add customer-specific controls.

Key definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): measurable signal (e.g., request success rate, p95 latency).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): target for an SLI (e.g., 99.95% availability monthly).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; allowable unreliability within a rolling window.
- Burn rate: speed at which we consume error budget.

1) SLO framework and catalog
1.1 Objective and measurement windows
- Use a 30-day rolling window as primary measurement for availability and latency SLOs unless service owner specifies 7-day for high-change environments.
- Secondary reporting uses 90-day for trend analysis and calendar-month for billing/contractual SLAs.

1.2 SLI definitions (examples)
- Availability (success rate): fraction of requests returning 2xx/3xx within expected response schema. Measured at the API-gateway and service ingress.
- Latency: p95 server-side duration (end of queue to response). For streaming endpoints, use 'time-to-first-byte' and 'median tail per-chunk latency'.
- Correctness: supervised evaluation sample for model outputs (applies to model-serving SLOs); measured via daily samplings and ground-truth prompt sets.

1.3 SLO targets (default catalog)
- API Gateway Availability: "99.95%" (30-day)
- Inference Service Availability (standard models): "99.9%" (30-day)
- Critical routing service Availability: "99.99%" (30-day)
- Inference p95 Latency (default seq_len=256): "<120ms" (30-day)
- Embedding generation p95: "<220ms" (30-day)
- Model-correctness regression: "No more than 3% degradation vs baseline on core prompt-set (30-day)"

Note: Service owners may propose a different target via SLO proposal process (section 4).

2) Error budget policy and burn-rate controls
2.1 Alerting and tiers
- Warning (soft) alert: when error budget remaining < 50% for the 30-day window. Notify service owner and SRE slack channel (#sre-alerts-soft).
- Elevated alert: when remaining < 25% or burn rate > 4x sustained for 1 hour. Page on-call and open incident chronicle ticket.
- Enforcement: when remaining < 10% or burn rate > 10x for 30 minutes, an "Error Budget Hold" is triggered and planned feature rollouts must be paused (see enforcement checklist).

2.2 Burn-rate calculation
- Burn rate = (observed bad minutes / total minutes) * (window length minutes / allowed bad minutes). Automations compute burn rate hourly from aggregated SLI time-series.
- Example: For a 30-day window and 99.95% SLO, allowed bad minutes = 0.0005 * (30*24*60) = ~21.6 minutes per 30 days. If we’ve accumulated 15 bad minutes in last 24 hours, burn rate = (15 / 21.6) * (1440 / 1440) = 0.694 -> 69.4% of daily allowance in one day.

2.3 Error Budget Hold checklist (enforcement steps)
1. Notify product and release managers and pause feature merges to production for that service.
2. Revert any non-essential recent changes (guided by deploy timeline).
3. Allocate SRE on-call to investigate root cause and implement mitigation (see runbook: high-error-rate).
4. Document findings in immediate incident note and schedule a detailed postmortem within 72 hours if hold persists beyond 24 hours.

3) Capacity planning & forecasting
3.1 Forecasting cadence and inputs
- Quarterly capacity review: each service owner submits a capacity forecast 2 weeks before the quarter close. Forecast includes expected QPS by endpoint, seq_len distribution, expected traffic growth, and major releases (marketing, partnerships).
- Monthly short-term runway check: capacity headroom for next 30 days evaluated by SRE/infra.

3.2 Sizing model and buffer policy
- Base sizing = observed P95 QPS over 30 days * cost-of-work multiplier (default 1.4 to account for burstiness).
- Buffer policy tiers: 
  - Critical services: 100% spare headroom (i.e., capacity >= 2x baseline).
  - Tier-1 services: 50% spare headroom.
  - Non-critical internal services: 20% spare headroom.
- Autoscale policy: prefer autoscale with min=safety-capacity, max=3x baseline for hosted deployments; Dedicated reserved pools should maintain explicit headroom based on contract.

3.3 Stress testing and verification
- Quarterly synthetic load tests (canary and full-scale) coordinated with product owners. Include model-sequence-length variation and KV-cache warmup tests.
- Required pass criteria: error budget consumption < 20% during steady burst test of 2x baseline sustained for 10 minutes; no p95 latency regressions > 40% vs baseline.

4) Reliability initiatives and project prioritization
4.1 Initiative classification
- Hotfix (P0): quick rollback or configuration fix; expected resolution < 8 hours.
- Tactical (P1): 1–3 week project (e.g., caching layer improvements, request retries optimization).
- Strategic (P2): 3–6 month investment (e.g., runtime kernel optimization, model quantization program).

4.2 Prioritization rubric (objective inputs)
- Expected error-budget impact reduction (monthly minutes saved).
- Cost efficiency: expected tokens/second cost reduction.
- Operational toil reduction (meetings, manual steps).
- Regulatory/customer SLAs impacted.
- Score initiatives on a 0–10 scale across dimensions; projects with combined score >= 25 prioritized for next quarter.

5) Incident review standards and postmortem process
5.1 Immediate post-incident steps (first 24 hours)
1. Triage and restore service (Runbook-first approach).
2. Create incident ticket and assign severity and owner.
3. Record timeline and communications in incident chronicle.

5.2 Postmortem template requirements
- Title, severity, service(s) affected, incident lead, timeline (with UTC timestamps), immediate mitigation steps, root cause analysis (5 whys + evidence), impact quantification (customers affected, error-budget consumed), action items (owner, ETA), and follow-up verification plan.
- Postmortem must be published within 72 hours of incident resolution for Sev >=P1.

5.3 Blameless culture and RCA expectations
- Focus on systemic causes and process or tooling gaps. Individual mistakes are documented but not the focus of remediation.
- Where human error is causal, produce a checklist or automation to reduce recurrence.

6) Operational tooling and observability standards
6.1 Dashboards and essential panels
- Per-service SLO dashboard: SLI timeseries, burn-rate, rolling window availability, top error traces, top endpoints by QPS, p95/p99 latency.
- Cluster health: GPU utilization, pod restart counts, queue lengths, KV cache hit rates.
- Canary vs production comparison dashboard for rollouts.

6.2 Alerting design principles
- Alert on symptoms (high error rate, high queue depth) and on business impact (drop in throughput, synthetic user failure).
- Avoid single-metric alerts; prefer composite rules (error-rate AND increased latency) to reduce noise.
- Include runbook link and pager duty rotation info in alert message.

6.3 Automation and tooling inventory
- Incident CLI: rwi (Redwood incident helper) — wraps kubectl, traces, and alert context. Examples: 
  - rwi status --service inference-api 
  - rwi traces --trace-id XYZ123 
- SLO agent: central Prometheus/metric-collector job pushes pre-aggregated SLI windows to the SLO service.
- Deploy verification: pipeline step that runs synthetic canary checks and blocks merge on failure.

7) Core runbooks (operational playbooks)
Note: Runbooks are action-first. If runbook steps do not resolve the event within the stated timeout, escalate to incident playbook.

7.1 Runbook: High error rate — inference-api
Trigger condition:
- Alert: per-minute 5xx rate > 1% for 5 minutes OR API Gateway error budget remaining < 25%.
Pager: oncall-sre -> primary -> secondary escalation.
Triage (0–10 minutes):
1. Check global SLO dashboard and observe whether errors are isolated to a single region/model.
2. Run: kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide | grep inference-api and check pod restarts and AGE.
3. Check recent deploys: rwi deploys --service inference-api --since 60m.
4. Retrieve traces for a sample error: rwi traces --service inference-api --limit 50 | jq '.errors[0]'.
Mitigation (10–45 minutes):
1. If a recent config/deploy correlates with start time, roll back to previous stable revision: rwi rollback --service inference-api --revision v2026-01-18.
2. Increase replicas by +30% temporarily: kubectl patch hpa inference-api -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":6}}' (adjust to service baseline).
3. If model-specific, disable warm cache policy or route to a cheaper, older model variant by updating routing policy: rwi routing set --service inference-api --variant fallback-small --weight 100
4. Add request-level rate-limiting at the gateway for noisy customers: rwi rate-limit add --customer-id 0x1234 --qps 10.
Follow-up (post-restoration):
- Create incident ticket, assign postmortem owner, and note whether error budget hold applied.
- Run targeted stress test to confirm resilience.

7.2 Runbook: Latency spike — p95 increase
Trigger condition: p95 latency > SLO threshold for 10 consecutive minutes and increased CPU/GPU queue depth.
Quick steps:
1. Check queue lengths on the routing service and model worker pools.
2. Inspect kernel-level metrics (GPU busy, memory pressure).
3. If kernel-bound, scale up workers or shift traffic to a region with lower utilization.
4. If caused by long-sequence traffic surge, apply request size gating: rwi gating set --service inference-api --max-seq 1024 --duration 30m.

Appendices
A. SLO configuration table (example values)
| service | SLI | SLO (30d) | alert soft | alert hard | owner |
| API Gateway | availability | 99.95% | remaining<50% | remaining<25% | platform-api@redwood.com |
| Inference-standard | availability | 99.9% | remaining<50% | remaining<25% | inference-team@redwood.com |
| Routing-critical | availability | 99.99% | remaining<60% | remaining<30% | routing@redwood.com |

B. Postmortem checklist (required fields)
- Executive summary (1–2 sentences)
- Timeline with UTC timestamps
- Root cause and contributing factors
- Immediate mitigation and long-term fixes
- Action items with owners and dates
- Verification plan and success criteria

C. SLO proposal process (how to change an SLO)
1. Service owner creates SLO proposal PR against the SLO catalog (repo: infra/slo-catalog). Include rationale, measurement method, historical SLI data, and proposed enforcement policy.
2. SRE review board reviews within 7 business days.
3. If approved, update central SLO service and notify downstream teams; run a 14-day validation window before changing enforcement policies.
